name: Pedro Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, totally fine. I'm into this topic, actually, so happy to talk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a big online retail fulfilment centre off the motorway junction, the kind where you don't walk the aisles. Little orange robots drive the shelving units, we call them pods, to my station, a light points at the bin, I grab the item, scan it, drop it in the tote. Ten-hour shifts, four days on. On a good day I do 330 picks an hour and I've got a podcast in one ear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm already working with robots, I find it interesting watching how they route. What wears me out is standing on the same square metre for ten hours, and the money. I share a flat with two mates on Canal Street, and I send my mum £100 a month, so I never get more than about two weeks ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, half the AI stuff was a sales pitch. But I'd say the robots we've already got at the fulfilment centre aren't hype, they're on the floor right now. Online I'd post something like, the hype died, the pick rate didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm stuck at a station with the pods for longer than I'd like. I use AI every day for planning my budget and studying, so for me it's a tool that stays a tool. The problem is the pay, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my online mechatronics course in the evenings, it's £35 a month. I'd apply for the robotics technician trainee spot when it comes up, they post two or three a year. And I'd keep the union card, because the pay talks matter whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, a bit bored at the idea of nothing changing. I wanted a bit of change, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the robotics technician job like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the ones in the yellow vests who go into the robot field when a pod drops something or a robot stalls. It's £3 an hour more and you're moving, solving stuff. There are about twelve of them for eight hundred of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send your mum money. What happens if that has to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd manage, she's got her cleaning job, but it's her rent help. It'd be the last thing I cut, I'd sell my games console first.

I'd post that the hype died but the **pick rate** didn't.
think: For me AI stays a **tool**; the problem is the pay, not the robots.
Nothing changing means I'm **stuck at a station** longer than I'd like.

Apply for the **robotics technician** trainee spot when it's posted.
Keep his **union card** for the pay talks.
feel: **Uneasy** about money and a bit bored at the idea of nothing changing.

fieldNote: He already **works with robots** daily and sees them as interesting, not a threat.
Sends his **mum £100** a month, which keeps him two weeks from trouble.
Twelve technicians for **800 pickers**: he knows the odds for his ladder.

steps.text: Keep the £35 a month online mechatronics course going
Apply for the robotics technician trainee post
Keep his union membership for pay talks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when unions need to get into the robotics side, training and pay for the techs. I'd say it in the group chat and online. Change is coming, so let's make sure workers get a cut of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine-ish, maybe better off. The pods are already here, the next step is robot arms doing the grab, and somebody has to maintain them. The thinking side barely touches me, except the scheduling, which is already done by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the tech trainee job, and use AI to drill fault codes and wiring diagrams every evening. I'd ask my shift lead for a week shadowing the techs. Maybe do some weekend phone repair for cash, I'm good with tiny screws.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, a bit excited. It's my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people at the other stations?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that's not fine. Most of the people near me aren't interested in robots, they're here because it's the job near home. If the robot arms come, eight hundred pickers becomes four hundred, and that's real people from our estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you be one of the four hundred who go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, of course, I'm not a technician yet. That's why I'm drilling the course. I reckon I've got a year or two to get across.

I'd tell the group chat workers should get a **cut** of the change.

steps.text: Drill fault codes each evening with an AI tutor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership of some of this, or at least a robot dividend for everyone. I'd say it online, definitely. If the machines do the work, everybody should share the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my plan breaks. AGI in 2028 means the AI can diagnose the robots itself, so a tech becomes someone who swaps a part when the screen tells them. Then 2031 the robots are good enough to swap parts on each other. My two years of study buys me maybe three years of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get the tech job as fast as possible, because three years of £3 more is still money. I'd save hard, put £200 a month away and stop the console games. And I'd get involved with the union on a robot tax, I'd go to the meetings and help with the posts because I'm good online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I always thought I was the one on the right side of the robots, and in this picture there isn't a right side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years where the hands are still human. Somebody has to plug in the new robots, rack the shelves, run the cables. I'd want to be that person, then I'd want to be out of there by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Out to where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, that's the scary bit. Maybe something with people, like teaching kids how this stuff works. I'm not a teacher, but I've taught half my shift how to use their phone apps.

I'd say online that if machines do the work, **everybody shares** the output.

fieldNote: The fast timeline breaks the one **plan** he trusted.
He sees the **three-year gap** as installation work for humans, then a cliff.
Unsure where he'd go next; floats **teaching** people tech.

steps.text: Move into the robotics technician job as soon as possible
Put £200 a month into savings and sell the console
Run online posts for the union's robot tax campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper transition, robot levy, training accounts, the lot. I'd be loud about it online. I'd say workers should be on the committee, not just bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI and robots around 2034 gives me time to go technician, then maybe move into the installing side, setting up robot sites for other companies. That's travelling work and the pay is better. It's still a tunnel with an end, but it's a long tunnel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the mechatronics course in year one and get the tech job. I'd use the AI tools to build a little portfolio of fixes and videos. And I'd start the emergency fund, £100 a month, so I can take a travelling job without panicking about the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but motivated. That's the version I could actually plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be setting up robots that replace people like your mates. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, honestly. If I don't set up the robots, someone from another town does. I'd rather be the one in the room saying, keep these ten people, retrain them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A union that covers the installers, because those are agency jobs mostly. And a bit of savings so I'm not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Free training, a shorter week, robot dividend by the end. I'd say it at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI and about 2039 for robots, I'd be 40. That's long enough to do a proper engineering qualification part time. I'd honestly feel okay about that one, the money's the only thing in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tech job, then start a part-time engineering apprenticeship in year two. I'd use the AI every day to study. And I'd keep the £100 to my mum going, and save around £100 for me as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but still uneasy about the money side. One broken boiler in my mum's flat and the savings are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the people who think you're too keen on robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm keen on not being poor. The robots are going to come either way, I'd rather understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you let the ten years slide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, that's not me. My risk is the opposite, I'd sign up for three things and burn out.

I'd tell the union we should aim for a **robot dividend**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It breaks the one plan I've got. What would help is training that comes with pay, and some sort of share for workers in what the robots make.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they actually know about the robots at their own work. You can't get ready for something nobody explains. Most of my shift doesn't even know the robot pods run on a schedule.

headlineQuote: You can't get ready for something nobody explains. Most of my shift doesn't even know the robot pods run on a schedule.
portrait: **Pedro** is 27, picks at a robot-served fulfilment centre and shares a flat with two friends.
He sends his **mum £100** a month and is never more than two weeks ahead.
He's curious and uses **AI daily**, studying mechatronics to become a robot technician.
He leans left and backs a **robot dividend**, while worrying for neighbours who don't move.
He stays mostly uneasy, but AGI by 2028 **breaks his plan** and alarms him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it breaks his plan to become a **technician**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** and a share for workers in what the robots produce.
